claim.pdf_says:
5) If the NEAREST-EVEN phrase is specified and the arithmetic value cannot be exactly represented in the resultant identifier, ... If two such values are equally near, the value whose rightmost digit is even is chosen.

    NOTE    This method is sometimes known as 'banker's rounding'.   [the NOTE is indented to the body-text indent of list item 5), i.e. a sub-item of rule 5]
claim.markdown_says:
5) If the NEAREST-EVEN phrase is specified ... the value whose rightmost digit is even is chosen.

NOTE This method is sometimes known as 'banker's rounding'.

6) If the NEAREST-TOWARD-ZERO phrase is specified ...   [the NOTE is flush at the left margin, detached from rule 5]
claim.why_it_matters: The NOTE is scoped to rule 5 (NEAREST-EVEN) in the printed standard. Flush-left placement between rules 5 and 6 reads as a note on the whole rounding-mode list rather than on NEAREST-EVEN alone. The same transcription indents NOTE 1 under item 1 on page 588, so the flush placement here is an inconsistency, not a house style.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED. The claim describes both sources accurately but the difference is pure paragraph indentation, and its load-bearing argument is factually wrong.

(1) Text is verbatim and correctly ordered. Rendered p591 at 300dpi and read the transcription. PDF: "NOTE    This method is sometimes known as 'banker's rounding'." Markdown line 12: "NOTE This method is sometimes known as 'banker's rounding'." Identical apart from a collapsed whitespace run. It sits between item 5) and item 6) in BOTH sources. Nothing is missing, altered, reordered, or moved across a rule boundary. Item 5)'s own text also matches verbatim (only the double space after "resultant identifier." collapses). The sole delta is the leading indent of one paragraph: ~4 spaces vs 0. That is formatting, which the verification rules exclude.

(2) Printed indentation confirmed, but it does not carry meaning here. In the PNG the word NOTE begins at the same left edge as item 5)'s body text ("If the NEAREST-EVEN"), right of the "5)" marker, so the PDF does render it as a continuation of rule 5. However "This method" is anaphoric to the sentence immediately preceding it, and that sentence is rule 5's round-half-to-even rule in both documents. The alternative reading the claim fears -- a note on the whole list -- is self-refuting: the list enumerates ten distinct rounding modes (AWAY-FROM-ZERO, NEAREST-AWAY-FROM-ZERO, NEAREST-EVEN, NEAREST-TOWARD-ZERO, PROHIBITED, TOWARD-GREATER, TOWARD-LESS, TRUNCATION, ...) and only NEAREST-EVEN is banker's rounding. No reader can misattribute it, and NOTEs are non-normative under the ISO/IEC Directives, so no compiler behavior can turn on this.

(3) The claim's key supporting argument is false. It asserts flush-left is "an inconsistency, not a house style," citing p588. Measured across all 53204 lines of specs/ISO_COBOL.md for the exact structure in question -- a NOTE paragraph immediately following a numbered list item -- the transcription is flush-left 92 times and indented 47 times. Flush-left is the MAJORITY convention, roughly 2:1, so p591 follows the house style rather than violating it. Verified analogues at line 2552 (NOTE after item 2, flush) and line 3678 (NOTE 2 after item 10, flush). Page 588 is the minority pattern and is also a special case: item 1) there carries an em-dash sublist plus a following continuation paragraph, and the ENTIRE continuation block is indented 4 spaces, so NOTE 1's indent is inherited from a multi-paragraph continuation block, not a NOTE-specific rule. Item 5) on p591 has no such continuation block. Page 591 also flattens the list markers themselves -- items 3) through 10) all sit at column 0 despite being indented from the margin in print -- so the flush NOTE is internally consistent with this page's own convention.

The claim's self-assigned severity of "cosmetic" is itself a concession that no meaning changes. No content discrepancy exists.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. The NOTE text is present verbatim and in the correct sequential position between rules 5) and 6); only its leading indentation differs (0 spaces in the transcription vs. the body-text indent of item 5) in print). Meaning is unaffected -- "This method" is anaphoric to the immediately preceding NEAREST-EVEN rule, and only one of the ten listed rounding modes is banker's rounding. The claim's premise that flush-left is an inconsistency is wrong: for a NOTE following a numbered list item, the transcription is flush-left 92 times vs. indented 47 times doc-wide, making flush-left the majority house style; the cited p588 case is the minority pattern and inherits its indent from item 1)'s multi-paragraph indented continuation block. At most this is an optional whitespace-normalization nicety, not a reconciliation finding.
